newsitem.title: MEXICO: Protesters attack Mexico election debate as sham.
newsitem.headline: Protesters attack Mexico election debate as sham.

text.p: Protesters jeered two front-runners for one of Mexico's top political jobs, saying they should not have held an exclusive televised debate Sunday night without inviting other candidates.

Mexico City votes on July 6 for its first elected mayor, a reform intended to promote democracy in a country ruled by one party for the past 68 years. The winner will be a prime candidate to contest Mexico's next presidential race in 2000.

But around 60 protesters gathered outside a hotel where the debate was held on Sunday said there was little hope for Mexican democracy if the favourite to win the mayor's race -- left-winger Cuauhtemoc Cardenas -- refused to face all his rivals.

"Democracy! Democracy!", the demonstrators shouted as Cardenas and his debating partner, ruling party candidate Alfredo del Mazo, arrived at the hotel for the confrontation, which was broadcast simultaneously on television and radio.

Cardenas had refused to invite conservative rival Carlos Castillo Peraza -- running second in most polls -- because Castillo had attacked him for handing over several acres of public beach to his mother while he was a state governor.
"The debate is anti-democratic, exclusive and against the constitution," said Maria Estela Gonzalez, one of the protesters. "Sadly, we are witnessing the defeat of democracy."
Inside the hotel, the two candidates traded insults about their earlier records as governors in a carefully controlled confrontation.
A rigid format negotiated by Cardenas's Party of the Democratic Revolution (PRD) and Del Mazo's PRI reserved most of the 60 minutes allotted for monologues by the candidates on various policy areas.

Del Mazo accused Cardenas of breaking his promise to debate with all the candidates, attacked him for allegedly promoting religious intolerance when governor of the state of Michoacan in the 1980s and said he represented a party of violence and confrontation.
Voters, he said, would decide "if we want our city to be a hostage to conflicts and blackmail or if we want our city to be what it ought to be -- optimistic and open to the world".

Cardenas, who left the PRI in 1987 to found his own party, retaliated by accusing Del Mazo of passing a law while governor of the state of Mexico which punished anyone criticising the governor with up to two years in jail.

He attacked the PRI as a party which "resolves problems by killing each other" and accused Del Mazo of being a personal envoy of disgraced former president Carlos Salinas de Gortari, presumably because Del Mazo served as ambassador to Brussels under Salinas.

The big absentee from the debate, conservative candidate Carlos Castillo Peraza, used a 15-minute interview slot with a local television channel immediately after the debate to criticise both his rivals.
